item.title: The Ripple Effect of Going for It
item.description: Can you learn to captain a yacht at 62 and turn it into a world-traveling lifestyle? Absolutely! Below, Sine Maria shares a first-hand account of her family’s latest charter with Dream Yacht in the Balearic Islands. Read on for an inspiring look at courage, partnership, and what happens when you say yes to a new adventure on the water. The Ripple Effect of Going for It On breaking into worlds you weren’t born into, and what happens when you actually do the thing. By: Good Life Designed and Sine Maria If there’s one thing I’ve learned from my mom, it’s that life has so much to offer and the limit of your world is only limited by your ability to keep expanding. In the middle of the pandemic, as part of our collective pause, she and I decided to go through the whole Good Life Designed program together again. It was through that process that she decided she wanted to be closer to nature, swim more, and learn how to sail. She didn’t grow up around sailing, knew it was costly and a bit of a boys club, but always admired the access it gave those who knew how. That hobby could take you anywhere in the world. The world of sailing requires a unique blend of resources, courage, technical education, practice, and willing crew members to go along for the ride and be there while you figure things out on your first trips alone. It thrives behind heavy yacht club doors that some are born with access into – but most don’t even know exist. The dream of being certified as a sailor has an even smaller niche- attracting those who thrive on the pressure to read and respond to the chaos of the elements at sea while holding the responsibility of passengers’ lives in their hands. Now that I have experienced the reward that comes with that kind of responsibility – I see the draw. Breaking Into a World You Weren’t Born Into I tried to look into data about women certified sailors but couldn’t find any credible data because no one seems to be particularly interested in that stat – however I can tell you there aren’t many. Sailing, just due to the nature of it, the time it requires, the unease that comes with the experience, especially as you’re getting your first solo trips under your belt, is enough to send anyone right over the edge. It’s heady, it’s overwhelming, it’s complicated, it’s technical, and it feels uncertain and dangerous before you’re skilled and experienced enough to feel truly comfortable and at ease on the water. When Pernille got the ping to learn to sail, the biggest question was how, as a 62-year-old woman, was she going to do it. She tried visiting yacht clubs but as someone who wasn’t interested in the social component and was really looking for the technical skills to captain her own ship, it didn’t feel like the best place to spend her time or money. The classes and day sail opportunities to get out on the water were nice, but if she really wanted to learn everything she needed to, she needed something different. She came across Nautilus Sailing, a week-long course in the Sea of Cortez that would teach you everything you need to know about sailing and cap off the week with a test that would certify you to sail on your own anywhere in the world. My dad at the time was in the most stressful period of his career, navigating his independent school and their 400 families through Covid. Using his coveted spring break to learn to navigate another set of uncharted territories felt not quite like the vacation he needed. But he took a leap of his own and joined her anyway. They spent a week disconnected from everything to focus on learning the thing that would later give them access to the life they live now – barely imaginable to them then. Heading out on what feel like once-in-a-lifetime week long sailing experiences all over the world with friends and family. item.title: French Polynesia Cabin Cruise: The Floating Boutique Hotel for Effortless Island Hopping
item.description: Imagine waking up in a comfortable suite aboard a premium catamaran. You stretch out on crisp sheets and wonder what spectacular view is awaiting you today. Will it be the majestic twin peaks of Bora Bora or the white sand beaches and tropical jungles of Huahine? You step on deck and sniff the air: today’s port is actually the vanilla-scented shores of Taha’a. That’s what life is like aboard a French Polynesia cabin cruise. Every day, you get to go on a new adventure. At night, you rest and relax in the comfort of a spacious cabin aboard a shared catamaran charter. For many travelers, the freedom to visit multiple destinations rather than be confined to a single resort makes a cabin cruise a much better option than a typical holiday on land. What Is a French Polynesia Cabin Cruise? A French Polynesia catamaran cruise or cabin cruise is a travel option where you book a private cabin with its own attached bathroom on a catamaran. Instead of chartering an entire yacht yourself, you share the vessel with a small group of other travelers. How Cabin Cruises Work The catamaran operates much like a small-scale cruise ship but with a personalized touch. Your captain navigates the islands, and an onboard steward prepares your meals. This vacation style eliminates the stress of trip planning, sailing logistics, and meal preparation. And since vessels are shared among travelers, cabin cruises are more affordable than booking Tahiti yacht charters . Why It Feels Like a Floating Boutique Hotel Unlike massive cruise ships that carry thousands of passengers, a catamaran hosts between 8 and 12 guests. This creates an intimate atmosphere, similar to that of a small hotel, except you also get to experience different destinations and activities every day. In French Polynesia, our cabin cruises are offered on the Bali 5.4, Lagoon 620, and the Fountaine Pajot Ipanema 58, each accommodating 12 guests. Comfort and Convenience: What Is a Cabin Cruise Like Onboard? Life aboard a cabin charter is defined by relaxation and comfort. Your catamaran features decks, shaded outdoor dining areas, and a forward trampoline net. This net is a great spot to lounge as the islands glide by. No jostling for sunbathing space on crowded beaches or lining up to rent gear from stands along the shore. You can get all the sun you want on deck, and the cruise includes the use of water sports equipment. You can step directly off the yacht’s transom steps into the water, swim, snorkel, or kayak to your heart’s content. Island Hopping Without Repacking or Airport Transfers With 118 islands and atolls spread across an area as vast as Western Europe, French Polynesia island hopping is all about discovering the unique character of each destination. However, having your base camp be a hotel or resort limits your options. It also means you have to go through a drawn-out process of getting there before you can visit each different island. Traditional travelers must pack their suitcases, check out of their resorts, take a taxi to the airport, wait in security lines, and fly to the next island, only to repeat the check-in process. Meanwhile, on Tahiti cabin cruises , you unpack your bags once on arrival. While you relax on deck or sleep in your cabin, the catamaran moves you between Tahiti and other destinations like Huahine, Raiatea, Taha’a, and Bora Bora. A Tahiti cabin charter eliminates the need for regional flights and ferry schedules, saving you both travel stress and vacation time. Space, Food, Privacy, and Seasickness: Honest Answers Before booking a sailing trip, it is normal to have a few questions about how things work on a boat. Here is what daily life aboard your shared luxury catamaran looks like. Space: Yacht cabins are smaller than hotel rooms, but they’re just as well-appointed. item.title: Top Sea Turtle Sanctuaries you can visit while sailing
item.description: You might have noticed that we’re a fan of turtles – they even inspired our logo. Dream Yacht’s appreciation of all things turtles emerged from our beginnings in the islands of the Seychelles, where Aldabra Giant Tortoises and many varieties of sea turtles are so well-loved. In celebration of World Turtle Day, sponsored by the American Tortoise Rescue non-profit since 2000, we’ve researched turtle sanctuaries and conservation projects at key yacht charter destinations around the world. There are many excellent sea turtle conservation projects and sanctuaries to be found around the globe. Visiting them and seeing sea turtles in their natural habitat can help us gain a greater appreciation for these amazing creatures, and also learn more about conservation efforts and how we can get involved. In nature, most sea turtle hatchlings won’t survive due to predatory birds who catch them during their arduous trek to the sea. The ones that do make it to the sea face adjusting to warm water temperatures and the threat of ingesting plastic or getting caught in carelessly discarded fishing nets. Only one hatchling in 1000 survives to adulthood to reproduce. Conservation to protect hatchlings is so very important to rebuild turtle numbers around the world. Sea turtles are also vital to the health of coral reefs and seagrass beds. Without sea turtles to graze and maintain these ecosystems there will be a decline in many other marine species as well. If you love marine life, use our research to plan your itinerary for your next bareboat yacht charter so you can sail, enjoy turtle watching and do some good at the same time by donating to successful turtle conservation programs. #savetheturtles St. Vincent & Grenadines Make for Tobago Cays Marine Park and its turtle nesting sites among the cays of Petit Bateau, Petit Rameau, Baradal, Jamesby and Petit Tabac. The Baradal Turtle Sanctuary is a protected area with green and hawksbill turtles. You can swim with them in the shallow, clear waters; regularly seeing them surfacing for air. Just be careful to keep your distance and not chase or disturb them. Puerto Rico Add the uninhabited island of Culebrita, which is part of the Culebra National Wildlife Refuge , to your US and Spanish Virgin Islands sailing itinerary . This refuge is one of many that make up the Caribbean Islands National Wildlife Refuge Complex. Each refuge in the complex plays a vital role in conserving the unique species and resources of the Caribbean. Culebrita’s six beaches and Playa Tortuga, also known as Turtle Beach, are a breeding ground for sea turtles. You’ll see leatherback and hawksbill turtles in the water but make sure you don’t interfere with them and keep your distance. During your time at this sea turtle conservation area, you can also enjoy spectacular snorkeling and diving opportunities, as well as spotting the many birds that reside here. Guadeloupe Sail to Jacques Cousteau’s Underwater Reserve, a protected underwater marine reserve surrounding Pigeon Island featuring vibrant coral reefs and gardens, and protected marine life – including green turtles and other species of sea turtles. With its 1,000 hectares of coral, tropical fish, turtles and humpback whales, there are plenty of diving opportunities – experienced divers can discover natural sponge covered shipwrecks. Marine technician oceanographer and cinematographer Cousteau spent his life studying the sea and sea creatures – discover more about the turtle conservation project when you visit Guadeloupe . Bahamas Visit the Exumas Cays Land & Sea Park, established in the 1950s, and watch turtles swim among the reefs at uninhabited Shroud Cay, which serves as a natural sea turtle nursery. The world’s first protected area of its type, it has a total ban on removing any shells, plants or wildlife from within the park on land and sea. item.title: What I Learned From Our One-Year Sailing Sabbatical
item.description: Chris DiCroce is an Amazon bestselling author, sailor, online educator, and speaker. He’s been featured in Sail Magazine, The Waterway Guide, Spinsheet Magazine, and various other magazines and podcasts. He spent 6 years cruising various parts of the U.S. and the Western Caribbean with his wife and dog, and 2 years traveling through Guatemala and Mexico. To learn more about Chris and his travels, visit mondovacilando.com . Read about his experience living on a yacht below… Have you ever wondered what it would be like to take a one-year sailing sabbatical and sail away from it all? Do you find yourself watching countless YouTube videos featuring bronze bodies and beautiful sailboats anchored in the turquoise waters surrounding some faraway island? I know exactly how you feel. For years, I also dreamt of warm breezes and salty waves. After a stream of layoffs at my job left me searching for answers, I decided to go for it. The only thing that needed to happen in order for this dream to become reality was to convince my wife Melody to get onboard – literally. After many late-night discussions, we came to the conclusion that life is short. Time is precious. We said, “What good is having a dream if you never go for it?” So, on a glorious weekend, I, Melody, and our dog Jet loaded up our 35-foot sailboat and hit the high seas for what was to be our one-year escape. Casting Off the Dock Lines We sailed south along the east coast of the United States, bound for Cuba and the Western Caribbean. Once the butter started to melt, we knew we were closer to our ideal latitude. We adjusted quickly to our new life. The concerns we had about the lack of space or how Jet would adapt to life on a sailboat faded. As a matter of fact, when we saw the sun rise over the city of Havana, any remaining doubts about whether our sailing sabbatical was the right decision drifted off with the seafoam. It was a morning we’ll never forget. Cuban immigration officials were both shocked and amused that we were sailing with a 50 lb. dog. They had a lot of questions about how and where he goes to the bathroom. Of course we all had a good laugh as Melody and I tried to explain, in our mediocre Spanish, that getting Jet to go on deck was proving to be a test of wills. But once the officials were satisfied we had all the correct paperwork and international health certificates, Jet got his stamp of approval. We spent fourteen days exploring Havana’s bustling streets. We discovered quaint local eateries, amazing art galleries, and off-the-beaten-track neighborhoods. When we left, we sailed west along the north coast in some of the bluest water I’ve ever seen. We anchored in deserted bays and sipped our Havana Club rum as we watched the sun tuck itself in for the night. We crossed the Yucatan Channel and spent three incredible weeks anchored in the Makax Lagoon in Isla Mujeres. We learned a little more Spanish and immersed ourselves further into our cruiser personas. In our minds, a one-year sailing sabbatical wasn’t much time. We wanted to experience as much as possible, so we moved often. And we kept moving. We kept exploring. We sailed south to Belize, where we snorkeled the out islands and took in the spectacular reef that is second only to the Great Barrier Reef of Australia. Melody and I were in the water at dawn and in our bunk before 9. Sailing With a Dog Jet seemed to love his new aquatic life as well. I mean, who wouldn’t love long strolls on deserted beaches and endless belly rubs from strangers in the beach bar? But sailing with a dog presents some challenges. He’s a shepherd and he sheds a lot, therefore, we vacuum constantly. And yes, there’s the bathroom issue on longer passages. Jet refused to use the fake grass pad that we put on deck for his potty breaks. He gave in a few times when there was no alternative, but more often than not, we planned our route and our stops so that it afforded us the ability to land a dinghy and take him to shore.
